title: forgetting a session, and the worktree that goes with it
asserts: a core that advertises `sessionDelete` makes a session stop existing, which `kill` never did: the row is gone from the store, so a later attach is an error and a `listSessions` no longer names it, and the worktree an isolated create made is reaped and reported. A killed session is still history to attach to and replay - that is the difference this scenario pins, and the reason the reap is on the delete path and not on the exit edge, since the work in a worktree routinely outlives the agent that did it. Without the frame a rust-mode delete dropped the client's own row while the daemon kept its own, so the session came back on the next list or adopt and its `<repo>-worktrees/<8hex>` tree was left for a sweep to find (juancode-lxe3, juancode-oe30).

steps.note: a plain session first: the delete has to work with no worktree in the picture
deleted while it is still running: the core kills the pty on the way, so a client does not have to sequence the two
both keys omitted, not null: this session never had a tree, and "nothing to reap" must not read like "the reap is pending"
the assertion that separates delete from kill: a killed session is still attachable and replays its scrollback
there is nothing left to come back for
now the half juancode-oe30 is about: a session with a tree of its own
kill first, so the exit edge gets its chance to reap the tree and must not take it
an exit is not a delete: the row survives it, and so does the tree
still listed after the kill, with the path a reaper reads
the tree is named and reported removed. A core that dropped the row and left the directory would answer worktreeRemoved: false and be caught here rather than by a `pnpm loose` sweep weeks later
and it is out of the core's own list, which is what stops it coming back the next time any client asks
a delete for something this core does not have
answered rather than dropped: a client that asked to forget a session it thought existed has learned something
